1.c4 c5 2.Nf3.strategy: Develops the king's knight, controls d4 and e5 and prepares a d-pawn break, which can steer the game towards an Open Sicilian with White's pawn on c4 instead of e4. Black has to decide early how to meet that break, and the game stays flexible for both sides.

1.c4 c5 2.Nc3.name: English Opening: Symmetrical Variation, Normal Variation
1.c4 c5 2.Nc3.background: ECO files 1.c4 c5 2.Nc3 as A34, the Normal Variation of the Symmetrical English; with 2...Nc6 it becomes the Two Knights Variation (A35), and 3.g3 then gives the Fianchetto Variation (A36).
1.c4 c5 2.Nc3.strategy: Develops the queen's knight and puts d5 and e4 under watch, which makes it harder for Black to break in the centre with ...d5. White intends to develop first and break the symmetry later, with a slow build-up and a pawn break in the centre or on the wing. The game is usually patient, and the symmetry can last for many moves.

1.c4 c5 2.g3.strategy: Prepares Bg2, which presses on b7 and the centre along the long diagonal, and keeps both knights' squares free. White builds a compact set-up first and decides on the centre later, at the cost of leaving e5 less watched than after Nf3. The game is quiet and manoeuvring.

1.c4 c5 2.b3.strategy: Prepares Bb2 on the long diagonal, aiming at e5 and g7. The plan is sound but slow: no knight is out yet, so Black can blunt the bishop or contest the diagonal at once.

1.c4 c5 2.d3.strategy: Prepares e4 with pawn support and frees the c1-bishop, for a closed set-up. It is solid but modest, and Black can take the centre before White has developed a piece.

1.c4 c5 2.e3.strategy: Opens the f1-bishop and prepares d4, so that White can recapture with the e-pawn. The move is solid but modest, and Black can set up freely or take space in the centre.

1.c4 c5 2.e4.strategy: Takes space with pawns on c4 and e4, clamping d5. The price is a permanent hole on d4, which no white pawn can cover any more, so Black aims pieces at it, a knight above all. The move is sound, but it hands Black a clear plan.

1.c4 c5 2.d4.strategy: Challenges the c-pawn before a knight can recapture on d4. After 2...cxd4 3.Qxd4 Nc6 the queen is attacked and loses a tempo, and after 3.Nf3 Black can hold the pawn with 3...e5, since 4.Nxe5 Qa5+ wins the knight.

1.c4 c5 2.b4.name: English Opening: Wing Gambit
1.c4 c5 2.b4.strategy: Gives up the b-pawn to deflect the c-pawn from the fight for d4. White gets open lines and quick development, but Black keeps a sound extra pawn and can consolidate easily, so the compensation is thin.

1.c4 c5 2.a3.strategy: Prepares b4, but spends a tempo on a rim pawn that does nothing for the centre or development. Black develops freely and takes space in the centre, and nothing in the position makes a3 urgent.

1.c4 c5 2.a4.strategy: Stops ...b5 and gains queenside space, but weakens b4 and loses time for development. Black develops freely.

1.c4 c5 2.f3.strategy: Prepares e4 but blocks the g1-knight's best square and weakens e3 and the e1-h4 diagonal. It develops nothing, and Black takes the centre at once.

1.c4 c5 2.f4.strategy: Takes e5 for a Dutch-style structure, but develops no piece and weakens e3 and the e1-h4 diagonal. Black develops freely or hits the centre at once, and White's kingside is loosened before the pieces are out.

1.c4 c5 2.g4.strategy: Gains kingside space but empties g2, opening the long diagonal towards the rook on h1. After 2...d5 the c8-bishop attacks the g4-pawn, and 3.cxd5 Qxd5 also hits the rook, so White must spend another move to save the rook.

1.c4 c5 2.h3.strategy: Takes g4 from a black bishop or knight but spends a tempo on a rim pawn that the position does not call for. Black takes the centre at once while White's development stands still.

1.c4 c5 2.h4.strategy: Gains kingside space and prepares h5, but neither challenges the centre nor develops a piece. Black takes the centre at once and develops freely.

1.c4 c5 2.Na3.strategy: Heads for c2, where it supports d4, or for b5, but on a3 the knight guards no central square and blocks the a-pawn. Black takes the centre at once while the knight needs a second move to reach a useful post.

1.c4 c5 2.Nh3.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, where it eyes f4 and g5. Once the d-pawn moves and opens the c8-bishop, ...Bxh3 and gxh3 doubles White's kingside pawns, and the knight does nothing for the centre.

1.c4 c5 2.Qc2.strategy: Brings the queen out before any piece has moved. It supports c4 and a later e4, but Black develops freely and can later gain a tempo by hitting the queen with a knight, while White's own pieces are still at home.

1.c4 c5 2.Qb3.strategy: Develops the queen before any piece and threatens nothing, since the bishop guards b7. It also takes b3 from the b-pawn, so a fianchetto is no longer possible, while Black develops with a free game.

1.c4 c5 2.Qa4.strategy: Brings the queen out early to a4, where it bears only on the guarded pawns on a7 and d7 and threatens nothing. Black develops freely, and ...a6 followed by ...b5 can harass the queen, while White's own development falls behind.

1.c4 c5.name: English Opening: Symmetrical Variation
1.c4 c5.background: So named because both players have advanced the c-pawn two squares. Alongside the Reversed Sicilian (1...e5) it is one of the broad categories of defence to the English Opening; ECO classes it as A30 to A39.

1.c4 c5 2.Nc3 Nc6.name: English Opening: Symmetrical Variation, Two Knights Variation
1.c4 c5 2.Nc3 Nc6.strategy: Develops the knight to its natural square, where it joins the c5-pawn in guarding d4 and also covers e5 and b4. Black commits to no pawn structure yet: a fianchetto, a clamp on d4 or the compact Hedgehog all stay possible. The price is that White decides what kind of game it becomes.

1.c4 c5 2.Nc3 Nf6.strategy: Develops the king's knight towards the centre, where it covers d5 and e4 and makes it harder for White to take space with e4. Black can mirror White, wait in the compact Hedgehog set-up, or strike in the centre with ...d5. White decides how sharp the game becomes, from quiet manoeuvring to open central play.

1.c4 c5 2.Nc3 e6.strategy: Opens the f8-bishop's diagonal and prepares ...d5, while keeping the compact Hedgehog set-up available. The cost is the c8-bishop, which stays shut in until the b-pawn moves, and no piece has been developed yet. It leads to solid, patient play.

1.c4 c5 2.Nc3 g6.strategy: Prepares ...Bg7, whose long diagonal presses on d4 and the c3-knight. Black aims for a solid fianchetto set-up, which can grow into the double fianchetto, hard to beat. The cost is that no piece is out yet, so White can open the centre early with d4.

1.c4 c5 2.Nc3 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7, from where the bishop presses on the long diagonal and e4. Played this early, it allows 3.e4, which blunts the diagonal and gains central space before Black has developed a knight. Sound, but less flexible than developing a knight first.

1.c4 c5 2.Nc3 d6.strategy: Opens the c8-bishop's diagonal and prepares ...e5. It is sound but commits the d-pawn before the knights, which leaves White free to choose its set-up. Less flexible than developing a knight first.

1.c4 c5 2.Nc3 d5.strategy: Strikes in the centre at once, but after 3.cxd5 the queen cannot recapture because Nxd5 wins it, so Black needs 3...Nf6. If White then plays 4.e4, winning the pawn back with 4...Nxe4 5.Nxe4 Qxd5 leaves Black with only a pawn for a piece. Playable but rare.

1.c4 c5 2.Nc3 e5.strategy: Takes the centre with both the c- and e-pawns, but leaves d5 without a pawn to control it. White can settle a knight there, and Black can challenge it only with pieces. Playable but rarely preferred.

1.c4 c5 2.Nc3 Na6.strategy: Aims for b4 or c7, but the knight on the rim does nothing for the centre, and ...Nb4 is met by a3 with a gain of time for White.

1.c4 c5 2.Nc3 Qc7.strategy: Brings the queen out before any minor piece, and 3.Nb5 attacks it at once, so it must move again and Black falls behind in development. Developing a knight first is more effective.

1.c4 c5 2.Nc3 Qb6.strategy: Hits b2, but the bishop on c1 guards it, so nothing is threatened, and 3.Nd5 attacks the queen so that it must move again. Black loses time while White's knight takes up a central post.

1.c4 c5 2.Nc3 Qa5.strategy: Lines up on the c3-knight and the e1-king, so the knight is pinned as soon as White's d-pawn moves. Nothing hangs, since the b2- and d2-pawns guard the knight, and White simply develops while Black's minor pieces stay at home.

1.c4 c5 2.Nc3 Nh6.strategy: Heads for f5 or g4, but the knight on the rim does nothing for the centre, and once White's d-pawn has moved, Bxh6 gxh6 doubles Black's pawns. Developing a knight towards the centre is more effective.

1.c4 c5 2.Nc3 a6.strategy: Prepares ...b5, but the break does not work yet: after ...b5 cxb5 axb5 Nxb5 White has won a pawn. Meanwhile no piece comes out.

1.c4 c5 2.Nc3 a5.strategy: Controls b4 and gains queenside space, but develops nothing and weakens b5 and b6 for good, which White can use while Black's pieces are still at home.

1.c4 c5 2.Nc3 f6.strategy: Prepares ...e5 but takes f6 from the g8-knight, weakens the e8-h5 diagonal and develops nothing. White enjoys the freer game.

1.c4 c5 2.Nc3 f5.strategy: Takes e4 in Dutch style, but loosens the kingside with nothing developed and opens the e8-h5 diagonal.

1.c4 c5 2.Nc3 h6.strategy: Prevents a later Bg5, which is not even possible while White's d-pawn stands on d2, and develops nothing.

1.c4 c5 2.Nc3 h5.strategy: Gains kingside space and prepares ...h4, but develops nothing and loosens g5 and g6.

1.c4 c5 2.Nc3 b5.strategy: Offers a pawn that White simply takes with 3.Nxb5 or 3.cxb5, since nothing guards b5. Black has no lead in development or other compensation to show for it.

1.c4 c5 2.Nc3 g5.strategy: Opens the long diagonal to the h8-rook and puts the pawn on the c1-bishop's diagonal. After 3.d4 cxd4 4.Qxd4 the queen attacks the rook and Bxg5 is in the air, so Black loses the pawn or weakens the kingside further.

1.c4 c5 2.g3 Nc6.strategy: Develops a piece and takes aim at d4 and e5 at once, while committing no pawn and no other piece. Black keeps every plan open, from copying White's fianchetto to taking space in the centre. The knight also stands on the long diagonal, so White's bishop on g2 will not press on b7.

1.c4 c5 2.g3 Nf6.strategy: Develops the king's knight toward the centre, where it watches e4 and d5, and commits no pawn yet. The position is the same as after 1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 c5. The knight does not yet guard d4, so White keeps a free choice of set-up, while Black keeps the option of striking at once with ...d5.

1.c4 c5 2.g3 e6.strategy: Opens the king's bishop and prepares ...Nf6 and ...d5 behind a solid pawn structure. The price is a slightly cramped position: the c8-bishop is shut in behind the e6-pawn until ...b6 gives it the long diagonal. Black aims for a sturdy, flexible game and waits to see how White commits.

1.c4 c5 2.g3 g6.strategy: Mirrors White's set-up: the king's bishop will go to g7 and press along the long diagonal toward d4 and b2. Until it gets there, the diagonal to the rook on h8 is open, so 3.d4 cxd4 4.Qxd4 attacks it at once. Black should block with ...Nf6, since 4...Bg7 loses the bishop to 5.Qxg7.

1.c4 c5 2.g3 Qc7.strategy: Defends the c5-pawn and covers e5, leaving room for a flexible set-up. The queen commits before any piece is out, so Nc3 followed by Nb5 can gain time against it. The plain 2...Nc6 reaches similar positions without that exposure.

1.c4 c5 2.g3 b6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the queen's bishop and then either a compact set-up with the e-pawn on e6 or a second fianchetto on the kingside. The long diagonal is the problem: after 3.Bg2 the bishop hits the rook on a8, and 3...Bb7 loses the bishop to 4.Bxb7, so ...Nc6 usually has to come first. The plan is sound but slower than 2...Nc6.

1.c4 c5 2.g3 d6.strategy: Opens the c8-bishop and prepares ...e5 for a compact set-up. The structure is sound but passive: the pawn commits early and makes ...d5 cost an extra tempo, so White gets the freer game.

1.c4 c5 2.g3 d5.strategy: Challenges the centre at once, and 3.cxd5 forces a choice. Recapturing with the queen hits the rook on h1, but White blocks with a developing move and then gains time on the queen with Nc3; recapturing with the knight regains the pawn, but Bg2 and Nc3 press on it.

1.c4 c5 2.g3 e5.strategy: Takes the centre with c5 and e5 together; the position is the same as after 1.c4 e5 2.g3 c5. With no pawn on c6 or e6, d5 becomes a hole that Bg2 and Nc3 aim at, and White can prepare the d4 break with e3 and Nge2. Sound, but Black has to develop carefully around that weakness.

1.c4 c5 2.g3 f5.strategy: Stakes out e4 with the f-pawn and can be followed by a kingside fianchetto. With nothing developed yet it loosens e6 and the king's position, and White develops naturally for the freer game.

1.c4 c5 2.g3 Na6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, where it contests neither d4 nor e5 and needs another move to find a useful square. White gains time while the knight is still on its way.

1.c4 c5 2.g3 Qb6.strategy: Hits b2, but Bc1 covers it, and the exposed queen becomes a target: Nc3 followed by Nd5 attacks it with tempo while Black still has no piece developed.

1.c4 c5 2.g3 Qa5.strategy: Leaves d8 before a single piece is out and has no real target: the rook covers a2, and the d2-pawn closes the diagonal to e1. White simply develops.

1.c4 c5 2.g3 Nh6.strategy: Places the knight on the rim, where it eyes f5 and g4 but no central square. Once White's d-pawn moves, Bxh6 gxh6 doubles Black's pawns, and a knight that goes to f5 can be driven back by a pawn move with a gain of space.

1.c4 c5 2.g3 a6.strategy: A waiting move that prepares ...b5 but does nothing for the centre or for development. White builds freely.

1.c4 c5 2.g3 a5.strategy: Adds a second guard to b4 and gains queenside space, but leaves the centre and development untouched and turns b5 into a hole no Black pawn can cover. White develops with a free tempo.

1.c4 c5 2.g3 b5.strategy: Offers a pawn: after 3.cxb5 a6 Black hopes for open a- and b-files against White's queenside, but with no central pawn or developed piece behind the gambit, calm development meets it.

1.c4 c5 2.g3 f6.strategy: Prepares ...e5 but takes f6 from the king's knight and weakens e6 and the king's position with nothing developed. White develops freely or opens the centre against a loosened set-up.

1.c4 c5 2.g3 g5.strategy: Advances the g-pawn with nothing to support it. The reply 3.h4 hits it at once, and 3...h6? 4.hxg5 hxg5 5.Rxh8 wins a rook; even otherwise the kingside is loosened for good.

1.c4 c5 2.g3 h6.strategy: A waiting move that neither builds the centre nor develops a piece; the only plan it supports is ...g5, which loosens the kingside. White gains a tempo.

1.c4 c5 2.g3 h5.strategy: Prepares ...h4 to attack g3 and open the h-file, but costs a tempo with nothing developed and loosens g5. White answers 3.h4, which stops the idea and keeps the kingside shut.

1.c4 c5 2.d4 cxd4.strategy: Takes the pawn on offer. White can retake at once with the queen, but then loses time as Black develops with a gain of tempo; if White does not retake, Black is simply a pawn up. Black has little to fear from this early central break.

1.c4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.e3.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Liedmann Gambit
1.c4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.e3.strategy: A gambit: instead of retaking on d4 with the queen, White leaves the pawn and aims to open lines for the bishops. Black can capture again or just keep the extra pawn, and White's quicker development does not obviously make up for it.

1.c4 c5 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2.strategy: Completes the fianchetto: from g2 the bishop presses along the long diagonal on d5 and the queenside, and it shelters the future castled king. White controls the centre from a distance instead of occupying it.

1.c4 c5 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7.strategy: Mirrors White. The bishop on the long diagonal covers d4, the square White needs for a central break, and bears down on c3 and b2. Both sides now follow the same plan, and the game stays level and manoeuvring.

1.c4 c5 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.Nc3.strategy: Develops the knight where it works with the c-pawn and the bishop against d5: a pawn and two pieces watch the square, so Black's ...d5 break is hard to carry out. White keeps the pawn centre flexible and decides later how to open the game.

1.c4 c5 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.Nc3 Nc6.name: English Opening: Symmetrical Variation, Ultra-Symmetrical Variation
1.c4 c5 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.Nc3 Nc6.strategy: Black matches White move for move: the knight joins the c5 pawn and the g7 bishop in watching d4 three times, so White's d-pawn cannot break freely. The game stays symmetrical and strategic, a fight over the centre squares rather than for pawns.

1.c4 c5 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.Nc3 Nc6 5.Nf.name: English Opening: Symmetrical Variation, Three Knights, Fianchetto Variation
1.c4 c5 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.Nc3 Nc6 5.Nf.strategy: Develops the knight to a square from which it guards d4 and attacks e5, so Black cannot take central space for free. White leaves both the pawn centre and the fianchetto set-up open and waits to see how Black commits.

1.c4 c5 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.Nc3 Nc6 5.e3.strategy: Guards d4 and prepares to bring the knight to e2, from where it can support a later d4 break. A restrained, flexible set-up, but slower than taking space: Black gets time to build a central pawn structure.

1.c4 c5 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.Nc3 Nc6 5.e3.name: English Opening: Symmetrical Variation, Botvinnik System Reversed, with e3
1.c4 c5 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.Nc3 Nc6 5.e3.strategy: Takes space in the centre, denying White d4 and hemming in the g7 bishop for now. The cost is the d5 square: the c4 pawn, the c3 knight and the g2 bishop all watch it, and no black pawn can ever guard it again.

1.c4 c5 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.Nc3 Nc6 5.Nf.name: English Opening: Symmetrical Variation, Full Symmetry Line
1.c4 c5 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.Nc3 Nc6 5.Nf.strategy: Completes the mirror: the knight develops and covers d5 and e4, so Black can answer any central advance. Black keeps every option open and asks whether White's extra tempo is worth anything in a position with no pawn weaknesses.

1.c4 c5 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.Nc3 Nc6 5.Nf.name: English Opening: Symmetrical Variation, Botvinnik System Reversed, with Nf3
1.c4 c5 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.Nc3 Nc6 5.Nf.strategy: Claims the centre at once, the pawn held by knight and bishop. White's knight loses d4, and the g7 bishop is blocked by its own pawn. As after e3, d5 becomes a hole that Black has to live with, now with White's knight already developed.
Gets the king to safety behind the fianchetto bishop before anything happens in the centre. The rook comes to the f-file, from where the f-pawn can later strike at e5.

1.c4 c5 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.Nc3 Nc6 5.Nf.name: English Opening: Symmetrical Variation, Botvinnik System Reversed, with Nf3
1.c4 c5 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.Nc3 Nc6 5.Nf.strategy: Supports e5 with a pawn and frees the knight and bishop from its defence. Black builds a solid chain but accepts a narrower position: the g7 bishop is hemmed in by its own pawn and d5 is a hole for White's pieces to use.

1.c4 c5 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.Nc3 Nc6 5.Nf.name: English Opening: Symmetrical Variation, Botvinnik System Reversed, with Nf3
1.c4 c5 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.Nc3 Nc6 5.Nf.strategy: Develops the knight to e7, where it covers d5 and leaves the d-pawn free to advance two squares. The price is that e5 is defended by pieces only, so Black has less of a solid chain than after the pawn move but more elasticity.

Castles into the safety of the fianchetto, the same set-up Black has. With the kings secure, the fight moves to the centre, and the first side to find a good pawn break gets the initiative in an otherwise level position.

Copies White. The position is now fully symmetrical, with both kings safe behind fianchettoed bishops and no weaknesses on either side, so the game is decided by who handles the manoeuvring and the central pawn breaks better.

1.c4 c5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3.name: English Opening: Symmetrical Variation, Two Knights, Fianchetto Variation
1.c4 c5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3.strategy: Chooses the fianchetto over an immediate d4 break, controlling the centre from a distance with the bishop and the c3 knight. A quiet, manoeuvring game follows, in which White gives Black time to set up in the same way.

1.c4 c5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 g6.strategy: Mirrors the fianchetto and prepares a bishop on g7 which, with the c5 pawn and the knight on c6, keeps d4 under triple watch. White cannot take the centre with the d-pawn at will.

1.c4 c5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2.strategy: Puts the bishop on the long diagonal, where it works with the c4 pawn and the c3 knight against d5, and prepares to castle behind it. A solid, flexible set-up in which White has not yet committed the centre.

1.c4 c5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2 Bg7.strategy: Completes Black's fianchetto as a mirror of White's: the bishop eyes the c3 knight and the d4 square. The position is symmetrical and level, with neither side having weaknesses to attack.
